exercises.question: Black to move. You played 4...Nxe4 and White answered 5.Nxe4, so you are a piece down for a pawn. Find the forcing move that wins the piece back.
exercises.explanation: This is the 'fork trick'. 5...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4 at the same time; White can save only one. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 material is level and Black has a free, central position. Every other move simply leaves Black a piece down.

wrong.why: A quiet developing move while a piece down — White keeps the extra knight.
One square short: it attacks nothing, and White stays a piece up.

exercises.hint: Which pawn move attacks two white pieces at once?
exercises.objective: Look for forcing moves (attacks on two pieces) first when material is missing.

exercises.question: Black to move. In the Fajarowicz Gambit (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ne4 4.Nf3 d6 5.exd6 Bxd6), White has just centralised the knight with 6.Nd4?. It is defended by the queen. Calculate, and win material.
exercises.explanation: Your bishop on d6 stands between your queen and the knight on d4. Move it with check: 6...Bb4+! The check must be answered first, and every answer puts a piece on d2, cutting the line between White's queen and the knight. After 7.Nd2 Qxd4 (or 7.Bd2 Nxd2 8.Nxd2 Qxd4) Black has won a knight. To find it you must look one move past the check and ask what the reply blocks.

wrong.why: It eyes f2, but after 7.Nf3 White simply keeps the extra pawn.
It threatens f2, but 7.g3 defends and nothing has been won.

exercises.hint: Your bishop is in front of your queen. Can it move with check?
exercises.objective: Use an in-between check to cut a defender's line before capturing.

exercises.question: White to move and mate in two.
exercises.explanation: This is the finish of Morphy's famous Opera game (Paris, 1858). 16.Qb8+!! deflects the knight from d7; after 16...Nxb8 17.Rd8# the rook mates, guarded by the bishop on g5, because the black queen and bishop block their own king. Forcing moves first: the queen sacrifice is a check, so it must be examined even though it 'loses' the queen.

wrong.why: Strong, but not mate; Black can defend with ...f6 and play on.
The rook trade gives up the mating pattern and allows Black to untangle.

exercises.hint: Which black piece guards d8? Can you force it away with check?
exercises.objective: Examine every check, including sacrifices, before quieter moves.

exercises.question: White to move and mate in four. Visualise the whole line before you move.
exercises.explanation: 'Philidor's legacy': 30.Nf7+ Kg8 31.Nh6+ (double check from knight and queen, so the king must move) Kh8 (31...Kf8 32.Qf7#) 32.Qg8+! Rxg8 33.Nf7#, a smothered mate. Each move is a check, which keeps Black's choices to one or two — that is what makes a four-move line calculable.

wrong.why: 30...Kxg8! — the king, not the rook, takes, and there is no follow-up.
Threatens mate but gives Black a tempo; the forced mate is gone.

exercises.hint: Use knight checks to bring the king back to h8, then sacrifice on g8.
exercises.objective: Calculate a sequence of checks to the end, picturing where every piece stands.

exercises.question: White to move. The pawn on f6 and a queen on h6 would mate on g7. Find the forcing way to make the idea work.
exercises.explanation: 20.Qh6? at once fails to 20...Qxd1+, because the black queen both escapes and checks. So first remove it: 20.Rxd8 Raxd8 and only now the quiet 21.Qh6!, after which nothing stops Qg7# — Black's 21...Rd1+ 22.Bxd1 only delays it. A quiet move in the middle of a forcing line is easy to miss; look for it when the threat it creates cannot be parried.

wrong.why: 20...Qxd1+ — the queen you wanted to deflect takes your rook with check.
Too slow; Black trades on d1 and the mating idea disappears.

exercises.hint: Which black piece can stop Qg7#? Remove it with a forcing move first.
exercises.objective: Find a quiet move inside a forcing sequence after removing the only defender.

exercises.question: White to move. Count the attackers and defenders of the pawn on d5. Can you win it? Play the right capture.
exercises.explanation: d5 is attacked three times (Nc3, Bf3, Rd1) and defended twice (Nf6, Be6), so White wins it — provided the cheap pieces capture first. 15.Nxd5 Nxd5 16.Bxd5 Bxd5 17.Rxd5 leaves White a clean pawn up. Starting with the rook, 15.Rxd5?, gives up a rook for a knight because every recapture is by a cheaper piece.

wrong.why: 15...Nxd5 16.Nxd5 Bxd5 17.Bxd5 — you have traded a rook for a pawn and a knight.

exercises.hint: Count, then capture with the least valuable attacker first.
exercises.objective: Count a capture sequence and order the captures from cheapest to most valuable.

exercises.question: White to move. Both sides have a passed pawn. Count the tempi: should you race with the a-pawn or stop the h-pawn first?
exercises.explanation: Count: the h3-pawn needs two moves to queen, the a4-pawn four. In a race Black queens first (45.a5? h2 46.a6 h1=Q). But the white king is inside the h-pawn's 'square': 45.Kf1 h2 46.Kg2 catches it, and then the a-pawn walks home because the black king is far outside its square.

wrong.why: 45...h2 and Black queens two moves before you do.
One step too slow: 45...h2 and the pawn cannot be caught.

exercises.hint: How many moves does each pawn need? Can your king reach h1 or g2 in time?
exercises.objective: Count tempi in a pawn race before pushing.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's queen has just captured on d7. Recapture is natural — but is there something better first?
exercises.explanation: An intermediate move: 18...Rxe1+! takes a whole rook with check (the bishop on c1 blocks the a1-rook), and only after 19.Kh2 does Black recapture the queen with 19...Rxd7. Black ends up a rook ahead. The automatic 18...Rxd7 19.Rxe8+ Nxe8 just trades everything off.

wrong.why: Recaptures, but 19.Rxe8+ follows and the position is level.
Also recaptures, but leaves your e8-rook hanging to 19.Rxe8+.

exercises.hint: Before recapturing, look for a capture that comes with check.
exercises.objective: Look for an in-between check before making the obvious recapture.

exercises.question: Black to move. You can queen at once with 52...b1=Q. Count what happens next, then find the move that wins.
exercises.explanation: 52...b1=Q? 53.e8=Q+ gives White a queen too, and with checks available the game is drawn. 52...Kf7! takes e8 away: if 53.e8=Q+ Kxe8, and otherwise Black collects the e-pawn; either way the b-pawn then queens and Black is a queen up. Calculation includes counting what the opponent does with his tempo.

wrong.why: 53.e8=Q+ — White queens with check and it is queen against queen.

exercises.hint: What is White threatening to do on the very next move?
exercises.objective: In a race, include the opponent's best reply before queening.

exercises.question: Black to move. Taking the h4-pawn looks natural. Count the race first, then play the winning move.
exercises.explanation: Count: the a-pawn needs three moves, the white c-pawn four, and the white king on d5 is outside the a-pawn's square. 50...a3! 51.c5 a2 52.c6 a1=Q wins easily. 50...Kxh4? spends the decisive tempo: 51.c5 a3 52.c6 a2 53.c7 a1=Q 54.c8=Q and both sides have a queen.

wrong.why: Grabbing costs a tempo; White queens right after you and the game is drawn.

exercises.hint: How many moves does each passed pawn need to queen?
exercises.objective: Count tempi in a pawn race instead of grabbing material.

exercises.question: Black to move. After 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.Bg5 cxd4, White has jumped into the centre with 5.Ne5?. Find the forcing move that wins material.
exercises.explanation: Forcing moves first, and queen checks are the most forcing of all. 5...Qa5+! checks the king along the a5-e1 diagonal (White's d-pawn has gone) and attacks the knight on e5 along the fifth rank, with the bishop on g5 behind it. White must answer the check, for example 6.Bd2 or 6.Nd2, and then 6...Qxe5 wins a whole piece. A developing move such as 5...Nc6 lets White off the hook.

wrong.why: Natural development, but you miss the queen check that wins a piece.
It attacks the knight, but there is no check: 6.Nf3 and White is fine.

exercises.hint: Which queen move gives check and attacks the knight at the same time?
exercises.objective: Scan queen checks for double attacks that win material.
